spots.name: Plaza de la Trinidad
spots.label: Plaza de la Trinidad

text.access_note: This looks like an open public square, but check local signs for any restrictions.
text.description: Plaza de la Trinidad is a town square in Cartagena, and it is an easy first stop for a phone photographer. Squares like this work well because everything is at eye level: building fronts, open paving, trees or benches if there are any, and people crossing the space. That gives you a ready-made scene with depth and a sense of place. Start with the whole square in view, then move in on details. Look for a strong foreground such as a bench edge, a lamp post or a patch of sunlit paving, and place the buildings behind it. Wait a moment for people to walk through the frame, which makes the picture feel lived-in. If it is busy, a few well-timed shots of figures crossing the open space often work better than trying to keep the square empty. Take one wide shot, one at the default lens (1x) with a clear subject, and one close detail such as a doorway, a colourful wall or a shaded corner. Keep the phone level, since straight lines on buildings look odd when tilted. This note sticks to what you can see and photograph on the spot.
text.directions_text: Use the map to find Plaza de la Trinidad. No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so get there on foot or by whichever local transport you prefer. From there the middle of the square is about 37 m to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Plaza de la Trinidad is a square in Cartagena.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole square, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. If you have a telephoto (2x-5x), use it from where you stand to pick out a single detail on the far side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and sunlit walls keep their colour. Try a Live Photo while people walk through, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the buildings' vertical edges with them so they stay straight. Put some paving or a bench in the foreground, and leave the people crossing the square as part of the scene. Then move closer for one detail shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. That gives you the full width of the square with the buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows than midday. If the light drops, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something.

spots.name: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas
spots.label: Castillo San Felipe

text.access_note: Calle de la Media Luna is a public street; the fort itself appears to be a visitor site where entry and tunnel access may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.description:
Castillo San Felipe de Barajas is the great fortress of Cartagena. It sits on Cerro San Lázaro, a hill that once let the Spanish watch for attackers coming by land or sea. Building began in 1639 and the fort was expanded in the years after, under Spanish supervision and with African slave labour. It was first called the Castillo de San Lázaro. The plan is triangular, with walls that are wide at the base and narrow towards the top, and the castle stands about 41 metres above sea level. UNESCO listed it in 1984, together with Cartagena's historic centre.

This spot suggests a calm way to photograph it from outside. Those rooftops give the picture scale and a sense of the fort looming over the old town. It is also a free alternative to the ticketed ramparts.

If you want the wider view from inside, the fort's own walls give a panorama of the flag, the city and the Caribbean coast. Only some of the tunnels are open, so check on arrival. The hill has very little shade, so a morning or late-afternoon visit is more comfortable.
text.directions_text: Head for Getsemaní and look for Calle de la Media Luna, where the old wall sections run. From there the fort lies to the east, about 4 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: The fort stands on Cerro San Lázaro in Cartagena.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to include the rooftops, wall and hilltop fort together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the fort's walls. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of street and rooftops, as it makes the fort look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fort to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out the stonework. Take a few shots with different zoom levels so you can pick the best one later.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fort on the upper third, with the rooftops filling the lower part. Keep the horizon level. If you also visit the fort itself, the walls give a wide panorama with the flag and the coast, and the Túnel Magistral entrance frames the approach to the hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Calle de la Media Luna (along the remaining wall sections of Getsemaní, toward the fort on the hill). The fort on its hill seen across the Getsemaní wall, with the colonial rooftops in the foreground. The fort sits on its hill beyond the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when there is less glare and it is more comfortable to be out in the open. Late afternoon may suit best, as the sun should be behind you and fall on the fort.

spots.alt: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, Cartagena: the great fortress of Cartagena. Photo spot

spots.name: Bocagrande
spots.label: Bocagrande

text.access_note: Plaza Bocagrande is described as a free, open balcony, but check the official site before you go to confirm it is still open to the public.
text.description:
Bocagrande is the high-rise seaside district on the peninsula just south of Cartagena's walled city. Its name comes from the wide channel mouth between El Laguito and the island of Tierra Bomba. It is known for big hotels, apartment towers and a long beach, so the photo here is the skyline: a line of tall glass and concrete against the Caribbean. One of its towers, at the Hotel Estelar, rises to 202 m and is said to be the tallest in Colombia. The district is also split into zones, including Castillogrande, South Bocagrande and El Lagüito, each with its own feel.

The best way to capture it on a phone is to look along the shore from the balcony at Plaza Bocagrande. A guide describes it as an open balcony with unobstructed views of the sea and the towers. Aim for sunset, which one guide names as the best light. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines, and let the towers sit on one side of the frame with sea and sky filling the rest. If you want the old city walls in the same picture, a second viewpoint, Terraza Municipal, looks across the small bay with the walls and the towers together. Check that either spot is still open to the public before you plan your visit.
text.directions_text: The walled city (Ciudad Amurallada) lies just north of Bocagrande, and the peninsula sits directly south of it. Head for Plaza Bocagrande. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: Bocagrande sits on the peninsula immediately south of the walled city of Cartagena, between the old centre and the Caribbean shore.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole skyline and the sea in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the towers. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single tall building or a slice of the waterfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset sky keeps its colour. If the phone offers night mode, use it once the light fades and hold the phone against the railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on the lower third line so the towers and sky get most of the picture. Include a little of the balcony edge or some people in the foreground to give a sense of scale. If you want the old city walls behind the towers, Terraza Municipal is an alternative viewpoint across the small bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plaza Bocagrande. Looking out from a balcony toward the Caribbean with Bocagrande's high-rise skyline rising along the shore. At the balcony looking out toward the Caribbean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, according to one guide. Arrive a little early so you can find a spot at the balcony and try a few frames as the light changes.

spots.alt: Bocagrande, Cartagena: the high-rise seaside district. Photo spot
